name: Magic Squares V: The Counting Function of Semi-Magic Squares of Every Order
description:
## Motivation

The magic-square programme already on this platform works at fixed small orders: MacMahon's enumeration of the $3\times3$ squares, both the magic count $M_{3}(3e)=2e^{2}+2e+1$ and the semi-magic count $H_{3}(t)=3\binom{t+3}{4}+\binom{t+2}{2}$; the classification of the normal $3\times3$ squares; and the counts of the panmagic and symmetric order-three classes. Each of those is a statement about a **single** order.

This mission changes the axis. It asks what the counting function does when the order itself is allowed to vary, and answers with the structural theorem on which the subject is organised — one that separates the semi-magic squares from every other class in the family.

**Timeline.**

- **1915.** MacMahon determines $H_{3}$ and $M_{3}$ explicitly by hand-combinatorial methods [MacMahon 1960].
- **1966.** Anand, Dumir and Gupta, studying a combinatorial distribution problem, conjecture that $H_{n}(t)$, as a function of the line sum $t$, is a polynomial of degree $(n-1)^{2}$ for every order $n$ [Anand-Dumir-Gupta 1966].
- **1973.** The conjecture is proved independently by Ehrhart, from the theory of linear Diophantine systems [Ehrhart 1973], and by Stanley, from linear homogeneous Diophantine equations and the magic labelings of graphs [Stanley 1973].
- **1980.** Spencer publishes an elementary proof [Spencer 1980].
- **2002--2003.** Beck and Pixton compute the Ehrhart polynomial of the Birkhoff polytope explicitly at order four [Beck-Pixton 2002]. Beck, Cohen, Cuomo and Gribelyuk extend the structural picture to the magic, symmetric and pandiagonal counting functions, which turn out to be **quasi-polynomials** rather than polynomials [BCCG 2003].

The quasi-polynomial/polynomial split is the point of the mission, so it is worth saying what it is before anything else is proved. A **quasi-polynomial** of degree $d$ and period $m$ is a function of $t$ that agrees with a degree-$d$ polynomial on each residue class modulo $m$, with the polynomials differing between classes. A polynomial is the case $m=1$. For the magic squares themselves the values genuinely depend on $t$ modulo a period — at order three the count $M_{3}(t)$ vanishes unless $3\mid t$ — and the same phenomenon is visible in every other class. For $H_{n}$ it does not happen at all.

## Setting

An **$n\times n$ semi-magic square of line sum $t$** is an $n\times n$ array of nonnegative integers in which every row and every column sums to $t$. Entries may repeat, and no condition is placed on the diagonals. Write $H_{n}(t)$ for the number of such arrays.

In Lean the array is a `Square n ℕ`, that is, a `Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) ℕ`; the condition is `IsSemiMagic M t`, which asks for every `rowSum` and every `colSum` to equal `t`; and the counting function is `semiMagicCount n t`, the cardinality of the finset of all arrays over `Fin (t + 1)` satisfying `IsSemiMagic`. Restricting the entries to `Fin (t + 1)` loses nothing, because an entry of a square of line sum $t$ is at most $t$.

Dividing by $t$ turns such an array into a **doubly stochastic matrix** — a matrix of nonnegative reals in which every row and every column sums to $1$. So $H_{n}(t)$ is equally the number of **lattice points** in the $t$-fold dilation of the **Birkhoff polytope** $B_{n}$, the polytope of doubly stochastic $n\times n$ matrices. Two geometric facts about $B_{n}$ are what the mission is really about. Its dimension is $(n-1)^{2}$: the $n^{2}$ entries satisfy $2n$ line equations, of which exactly one is dependent, since the sum of the row sums equals the sum of the column sums. And its vertices are the $n!$ permutation matrices, by the Birkhoff-von Neumann theorem, so they have integral coordinates. The mission is the statement that these two facts are visible in the arithmetic of $H_{n}$.

## Formalization targets

### Goal — the counting function is a polynomial

$$\exists\, p\in\mathbb{Q}[X]:\quad \deg p=(n-1)^{2},\qquad p(t)=H_{n}(t)\ \text{ for all }t\in\mathbb{N},$$
$$p(-n-t)=(-1)^{n-1}p(t)\ \text{ for all }t\in\mathbb{Z},\qquad p(-1)=p(-2)=\cdots=p(-n+1)=0 .$$

This is Theorem 1 of [BCCG 2003], stated there for $n\ge 1$; it is the shape of the truth rather than any particular closed form, so no future improvement in the explicit formulas can invalidate it. The three parts are not independent packaging: the degree is the dimension of $B_{n}$, and the two identities in the second line are the reciprocity law for lattice-point counting in a polytope, applied to $B_{n}$.

### The intermediate rungs

The goal is far from the easy cases, and the mission is laid out so that each rung is an independently provable statement.

- **Order one.** $H_{1}(t)=1$: a $1\times1$ array of line sum $t$ is just $[t]$.
- **Orders two and three.** These are already proved on the platform, as `MagicSquares.semi_magic_count_two` ($H_{2}(t)=t+1$) and `MagicSquares.semi_magic_count_three` ($H_{3}(t)=3\binom{t+3}{4}+\binom{t+2}{2}$, MacMahon's formula). They are included as references, not as targets.
- **Order four**, stated with the denominators cleared so that it is an identity between natural numbers:
$$11340\cdot H_{4}(t)=11t^{9}+198t^{8}+1596t^{7}+7560t^{6}+23289t^{5}+48762t^{4}+70234t^{3}+68220t^{2}+40950t+11340 .$$
The leading coefficient is $\tfrac{11}{11340}=\operatorname{vol}(B_{4})$, and the normalised volume $9!\cdot\tfrac{11}{11340}$ is $352$. This rung is the concrete order at which the general statement can be touched without any machinery.
- **Existence and degree, uniformly in $n$.** The polynomial exists with degree exactly $(n-1)^{2}$.
- **The reciprocity identity**, and **the vanishing list**, for the polynomial of the previous rung.

## Significance

*The result itself.* The theorem is what makes the semi-magic squares countable in closed form at every order, and it is the reason the semi-magic count can be tabulated as a polynomial while the magic, symmetric and pandiagonal counts cannot: a polynomial is determined by finitely many values, a quasi-polynomial is not without knowing its period. Both reciprocity identities are the same statement seen from the interior of $B_{n}$, which is why they are the part of the theorem most often used to *pin down* an explicit polynomial once its degree is known. The order-four polynomial in this mission has been verified numerically against direct enumeration on seventeen values of $t$; the verification is evidence, not a proof, and it is included precisely because the general statement is what has to be proved.

*Formalizing it.* The theorem has been known since 1973 and has an elementary proof since 1980; what does not exist anywhere is a machine-checked proof. Mathlib contains no Ehrhart theory, no quasi-polynomial machinery and no rational-generating-function toolbox — the string "Ehrhart" does not occur in it — so a formalization has to construct its own lattice-point-counting argument for this family of polytopes, or find an elementary route that avoids polytopes altogether. Either outcome is reusable: the same absence blocks the quasi-polynomial counting functions $M_{n}$, $S_{n}$ and $P_{n}$ of BCCG's Theorem 2, which the earlier missions of this programme approach only at order three, and it blocks the hypercube counts of their Theorem 3.

## Difficulty

The first idea anyone has is to interpolate: compute $H_{n}(t)$ for enough values of $t$ and fit a polynomial. This works, and it is exactly how the order-four rung above was produced — but it cannot prove the general statement. The degree is what is being asserted, so the number of values required is not known in advance; and for a statement with the order $n$ as a variable there is no finite amount of computation that settles it. The order-four rung is the case where interpolation is legitimate as a *target*; it must not be mistaken for a route to the goal.

The second idea is to import the geometry as a black box: a rational polytope dilated by $t$ has a counting function that is a quasi-polynomial of degree equal to the dimension, and the period divides the least common multiple of the vertex denominators. This is Ehrhart's theorem, and it is the textbook route to the goal. It is not available here, and reconstructing it in general is a larger project than the mission. The two statements that survive without it are the ones the mission asks for: the dimension and integrality of $B_{n}$, and the polynomiality of the count.

The part of the goal that has no counting interpretation at all is the second line. $H_{n}$ is defined on $\mathbb{N}$; the assertion that a polynomial agreeing with it there takes the value $0$ at $-1,\dots,-(n-1)$ and satisfies $p(-n-t)=(-1)^{n-1}p(t)$ is a statement about the *interior* of the polytope, and it is the part of the theorem that cannot be read off from the combinatorial definition. A solver who proves only the polynomiality and degree has not finished the goal.

## Formalization scope

The formalization commits to the following conventions.

- The counting function is `semiMagicCount n t`, defined as `Finset.card` of the arrays over `Square n (Fin (t+1))` satisfying `IsSemiMagic`. Entries are natural numbers, not integers and not reals; the statement is not about rational or real semi-magic squares.
- The polynomial is over `ℚ`, and it is quantified existentially. Negative arguments are handled by casting the integer into `ℚ` and evaluating there. Note for anyone drafting: `Polynomial.eval₂` cannot be used for the reciprocity, since it requires a ring homomorphism out of the polynomial's coefficient ring and there is no ring homomorphism $\mathbb{Q}\to\mathbb{Z}$.
- The degree is encoded as `p.natDegree = (n - 1) ^ 2`, with the natural-number subtraction, which makes the $n=1$ case harmless rather than degenerate.
- The hypothesis `1 ≤ n` is carried explicitly although the statement is meaningful at $n=0$; it is there to match the source.
- A trivializing formalization to avoid: replacing `∀ t` by a finite range, or replacing `semiMagicCount` by a smooth surrogate, would make the statement easy and empty. The universal quantifier over $t$ and the exact value of `natDegree` are what give the goal its content.

Reusable beyond this mission: any development of lattice-point counting in the Birkhoff polytope, of dilations of rational polytopes, or of quasi-polynomials. The vocabulary of the programme — `MagicSquares`, `MagicSquaresPandiagonal`, `MagicSquaresMostPerfect`, `MagicSquaresTransforms`, `MagicSquaresNormal3` — is shared with the earlier missions and is included in the proposal as reference items rather than redefined.

## Selected references

- H. Anand, V. C. Dumir and H. Gupta, *A combinatorial distribution problem*, Duke Math. J. **33** (1966) 757--769.
- E. Ehrhart, *Sur les carrés magiques*, C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris Sér. A-B **277** (1973) A651--A654.
- R. P. Stanley, *Linear homogeneous Diophantine equations and magic labelings of graphs*, Duke Math. J. **40** (1973) 607--632.
- J. Spencer, *Counting magic squares*, Amer. Math. Monthly **87** (1980) 397--399.
- M. Beck and D. Pixton, *The Ehrhart polynomial of the Birkhoff polytope*, arXiv:math.CO/0202267 — <https://arxiv.org/abs/math/CO/0202267>
- M. Beck, M. Cohen, J. Cuomo and P. Gribelyuk, *The number of "magic" squares, cubes and hypercubes*, Amer. Math. Monthly **110** (2003) 707--717 — <https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0201013>
- M. Ahmed, J. DeLoera and R. Hemmecke, *Polyhedral cones of magic cubes and squares*, arXiv:math.CO/0201108 — <https://arxiv.org/abs/math/CO/0201108>
